title: Septic Shock: Vascular Tone, Blood Distribution, and Cellular Dysfunction
summary: Why three patients with the same diagnosis have different circulations, how sepsis attacks arterial tone, venous capacitance, the capillary wall and the heart, and where fluids, vasopressors and source control stop working. Study material, not a protocol.
shareDescription: How sepsis attacks vessel tone, veins, capillaries and the heart, and why fluids and vasopressors help some septic patients and not others.

principles.title: Part I. Three septic patients, one label
body: Three adults with septic shock arrive on the same shift. Like the patients in the earlier chapters, they are hypothetical, built for teaching, and each weighs about 80 kg. Their numbers are illustrative and internally consistent, and every calculation is shown where it is used. Cardiac output values are given as if they had been measured; this chapter does not teach how to measure them.

Patient V is 58 and has had pneumonia with fever for six hours. Her heart rate is 118 and her blood pressure 82/38, a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of about 53 mm Hg. Her hands are warm, her capillary refill takes 3 seconds, her lactate is 4.2 mmol/L, her central venous pressure (CVP) is 6 mm Hg and her cardiac output is 7.5 L/min. Her hemoglobin is 12 g/dL, her arterial oxygen saturation 94 percent and her PaO2 70 mm Hg. Patient L is 66 and is on his second day of treatment for a urinary source. He has received a net positive fluid balance of 6 L in 24 hours, his weight has gone from 80 to 86 kg, and his hemoglobin has fallen from 13 to 10.5 g/dL without bleeding. He is edematous, needs more oxygen than yesterday, and holds a MAP of 66 on a vasopressor. Patient C is 71 and has biliary sepsis from a gallbladder that has not yet been drained. His heart rate is 125, his blood pressure 88/52 (MAP 64), his CVP 14 and his cardiac output 3.2 L/min. His peripheries are cold, his capillary refill takes 5 seconds, his lactate is 6.0 and his central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) is 55 percent. Echocardiography shows a globally weak left ventricle.

The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-pressure-not-flow) showed that blood pressure is the final common output of a circulation and that the same pressure can come from very different combinations of flow and resistance. This chapter asks what sepsis does to each part of that circulation, and why the treatments that help one of these three patients can fail or harm another.

principles.title: What the label means
body: The current consensus definition, Sepsis-3, states that sepsis "should be defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection." For clinical use it is operationalized as an acute rise in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more. Septic shock is the subset of sepsis in which circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities are severe enough to raise mortality substantially, identified by a "vasopressor requirement to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mm Hg or greater and serum lactate level greater than 2 mmol/L (>18 mg/dL) in the absence of hypovolemia."

The definition is built on organ dysfunction and on a combined pressure and lactate threshold. It says nothing about cardiac output, vascular resistance or filling. That is deliberate: it identifies patients at high risk of death, not a hemodynamic type. All three patients here meet the septic shock criteria, Patient V once she needs a vasopressor to hold her pressure, and yet their circulations are failing for different reasons.

questions.prompt: A woman with pyelonephritis has a MAP of 70 mm Hg without any vasopressor, a lactate of 3.5 mmol/L and new confusion. By Sepsis-3, does she have sepsis, septic shock, or neither, and what does the label tell you about her circulation?
questions.answer: She has sepsis if her new confusion and any other organ dysfunction together represent an acute SOFA rise of 2 or more from her baseline; the confusion alone may or may not reach that, depending on its depth. If she has no known preexisting organ dysfunction, Sepsis-3 allows her baseline SOFA to be taken as zero. She does not meet the septic shock criteria, because she needs no vasopressor to keep MAP at 65 or above, even though her lactate is above 2. The label tells you her risk, not her hemodynamics: she could have high flow and low tone, as in Patient V, or a weak heart, as in Patient C, and only further assessment would say which.
questions.causalChain: Sepsis-3 requires infection plus organ dysfunction; septic shock adds both a vasopressor need for MAP 65 or more and lactate above 2 in the absence of hypovolemia; her pressure is held without a vasopressor; the definition does not specify a hemodynamic pattern.
questions.assumption: That the infection is confirmed and the confusion is new and not explained by anything else.
questions.misconception: That a lactate above 2 alone means septic shock.

principles.title: One diagnosis, three circulations
body: Placing the three patients side by side shows how little the diagnosis says about the circulation. Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) can be estimated as 80 times the difference between MAP and CVP, divided by cardiac output, in dyn·s·cm-5. For Patient V that is 80 x (53 - 6) / 7.5, about 500. For Patient C it is 80 x (64 - 14) / 3.2, about 1250. The same diagnosis gives a resistance that differs two and a half times between them.

Stroke volume tells the same story from the heart's side. Patient V's is 7500 / 118, about 64 mL. Patient C's is 3200 / 125, about 26 mL. Patient V has a strong heart pumping into vessels that have lost their tone. Patient C has a weak heart pumping into vessels that are, if anything, clamped down. Patient L sits between them, and his problem is mainly where his fluid has gone, which Part IV examines.

Simple bedside ratios do not separate them. The shock index, heart rate divided by systolic pressure, is 118 / 82, about 1.44, for Patient V and 125 / 88, about 1.42, for Patient C. Two almost identical indices describe opposite circulations. The index flags that something is wrong; it does not say what. No threshold is quoted here, because the chapter uses the index only to make that point.

questions.prompt: You are told only that Patient V's shock index is 1.44 and Patient C's is 1.42. Predict whether they share a hemodynamic mechanism.
questions.answer: They do not. Patient V has a high cardiac output of 7.5 L/min, a stroke volume of about 64 mL and an SVR of about 500: a strong heart and lost arterial tone. Patient C has a cardiac output of 3.2 L/min, a stroke volume of about 26 mL and an SVR of about 1250: a weak heart and high resistance. The two indices agree because each is a ratio of a fast heart rate to a low systolic pressure, and very different combinations of flow and resistance can produce that ratio.
questions.causalChain: Shock index is heart rate over systolic pressure; systolic pressure depends on stroke volume and arterial tone together; a high flow, low resistance circulation and a low flow, high resistance circulation can give the same pressure and heart rate.
questions.assumption: That the cardiac output figures are accurate and that both patients are assessed at the same stage of illness.
questions.misconception: That septic shock is always warm, high-output shock.

diagram.caption: Figure 1. One diagnosis, three circulations. Patients V, L and C shown as three small circuits. V: MAP 53, cardiac output 7.5 L/min, SVR about 500, stroke volume 64 mL. C: MAP 64, cardiac output 3.2 L/min, SVR about 1250, stroke volume 26 mL. L: MAP 66 on a vasopressor, edema. V and C have almost the same shock index. Illustrative teaching numbers.
diagram.alt: Three simple circuit diagrams side by side, each with a heart, arteries, capillaries and veins. The left circuit, Patient V, shows a large heart output with wide arterioles and labels MAP 53, cardiac output 7.5, SVR about 500 and stroke volume 64. The middle circuit, Patient L, shows fluid leaving the capillaries into surrounding tissue, with labels MAP 66 on a vasopressor. The right circuit, Patient C, shows a small heart output with narrowed arterioles and labels MAP 64, cardiac output 3.2, SVR about 1250 and stroke volume 26. A note under V and C reads shock index 1.44 and 1.42.

principles.title: Four levels of attack
body: Sepsis attacks the circulation at four levels at once. At the arterioles it removes tone, so the same flow produces less pressure. At the veins it lowers capacitance tone, so blood pools in the unstressed reservoir and less of it drives venous return. At the capillary wall it increases leak, so fluid given into the vessels does not stay there. At the heart and in the cells it depresses contraction and may impair the use of oxygen.

Each of the three patients is dominated by a different level. Patient V's problem is mainly arteriolar and venous tone, Patient L's mainly the capillary wall, and Patient C's mainly the heart. Fluids, vasopressors and source control each act on only some of these levels, which is why each helps up to a point and then stops. Part II takes the arterioles, Part III the veins, Part IV the capillary wall, Part V the microcirculation and cells, Part VI the heart, Part VII the cause, and Part VIII the limits of support.

principles.title: Part II. Lost arterial tone
body: Arteriolar smooth muscle sets most of the resistance in the systemic circulation. Its tone is a balance between constricting signals, such as sympathetic noradrenaline, angiotensin II and vasopressin, and relaxing signals, such as nitric oxide. In septic shock that balance moves toward relaxation, and the vessels also become less able to respond to constricting signals. The result is vasoplegia: wide arterioles that let pressure fall even when flow is high.

Calling this simply low SVR misses the point. SVR is a calculated number that falls whenever flow rises relative to pressure. Vasoplegia is a property of the vessel wall: the muscle is not contracting, and it responds poorly when asked to.

principles.title: Why septic arterioles stop constricting
body: Several mechanisms have been proposed, and reviews of vasodilatory shock bring them together. Inflammatory signaling induces nitric oxide production in the vessel wall, and nitric oxide relaxes smooth muscle directly. ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the smooth muscle membrane open, which hyperpolarizes the cell and closes the voltage-gated calcium channels that contraction depends on. Circulating vasopressin, after an early rise, can fall to levels lower than expected for the degree of hypotension, a relative deficiency. And adrenergic receptors and their signaling become less responsive, so the same catecholamine concentration produces less constriction.

These mechanisms are not supported equally, and the review by Lambden and colleagues allows a rough grading. Nitric oxide has the strongest human support, though it is indirect: in patients with septic shock, drugs that block nitric oxide production raised blood pressure but increased mortality. Opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels rests mainly on animal work; blocking the channels improved hemodynamics in animal models, but phase 2 trials in humans showed no benefit. Relative vasopressin deficiency has been observed in patients, whose levels rise early in shock and then fall to subnormal levels after about 24 hours, but that this causes the loss of tone is still described as possible rather than proven. Reduced adrenergic receptor responsiveness has only limited human data, which suggest that the pattern seen in rodents may also occur in patients. What can be said is that more than one pathway is involved, which is why no single treatment restores tone completely.

principles.title: Patient V in numbers
body: Patient V has a MAP of 53, a CVP of 6 and a cardiac output of 7.5 L/min, an SVR of about 500. Her heart is delivering more blood than normal, and her pressure is still low, because the arterioles are offering little resistance to it. Her diastolic pressure of 38 mm Hg is the most striking part of her reading. Between beats, arterial pressure decays as blood runs off through the arterioles, and when they are wide it runs off quickly.

Low diastolic pressure is commonly read as a sign of low arterial tone. In patients with septic shock, Ospina-Tascón and colleagues found that low diastolic pressure combined with a fast heart rate was associated with worse outcomes, while neither value alone clearly identified that risk. That is an association, not proof that diastolic pressure measures tone, and other conditions, such as a slow heart rate or a leaking aortic valve, can also lower it. This chapter gives no threshold and uses Patient V's diastolic pressure only as a reason to suspect lost tone and then check the other numbers, not as a measurement of tone.

questions.prompt: Patient V's MAP rises from 53 to 67 on a vasopressor, her CVP from 6 to 8, and her cardiac output falls from 7.5 to 7.0 L/min. Predict her new SVR, and say what the pressure gain proved and did not prove.
questions.answer: Her SVR rises from about 500 to about 670. The vasopressor restored some arteriolar tone, so the same heart now produces a higher perfusion pressure, which matters for organs whose flow depends on pressure, such as the kidney and the brain when autoregulation is impaired. It did not prove that her organs receive more flow or oxygen: total flow fell slightly, and the pressure gain says nothing about how flow is distributed between and within organs. That needs separate signals, such as capillary refill, urine output, mental state and lactate trend.
questions.causalChain: Vasopressor raises arteriolar resistance and venous tone; MAP rises; cardiac output may rise, stay level or fall depending on venous return and the heart's response to afterload; organ flow depends on both pressure and local resistance.
questions.assumption: That the measurements were made at steady state and the cardiac output figures are accurate.
questions.misconception: That a higher blood pressure means better perfusion.

workedExample.title: Worked example: Patient V before and after a vasopressor
body: Before: MAP 53, CVP 6, cardiac output 7.5 L/min. SVR = 80 x (53 - 6) / 7.5 = 80 x 47 / 7.5, about 500 dyn·s·cm-5.
After a vasopressor: blood pressure 100/50, so MAP = (100 + 2 x 50) / 3, about 67. CVP 8, cardiac output 7.0 L/min. SVR = 80 x (67 - 8) / 7.0 = 80 x 59 / 7.0, about 670.
Pressure rose by 14 mm Hg while flow fell slightly, by 0.5 L/min. These are illustrative numbers; the direction of the change in flow differs between patients and is not claimed as typical.

principles.title: Why tone can resist catecholamines, and the case for other vasopressors
body: If receptor signaling is blunted and smooth muscle is hyperpolarized, giving more of a catecholamine produces progressively smaller gains in pressure. This is one reason septic vasoplegia can need very high catecholamine exposure. The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-pressors-inotropes) already covers how vasopressors and inotropes act on pressure and flow; the sepsis-specific point is about mechanism.

Vasopressin acts through its own receptors, not through adrenergic ones, so it bypasses the blunted adrenergic pathway. If part of the problem is a relative vasopressin deficiency, giving it replaces a missing hormone rather than simply adding more constriction. That was the physiological rationale for the VASST trial, which compared vasopressin with norepinephrine in septic shock. Its result is discussed in Part VIII, where the adjunct trials are taken together. The rationale is physiological; whether it changes outcomes is a separate question that only trials can answer.

questions.prompt: A patient is profoundly hypotensive with warm peripheries after cardiopulmonary bypass, and another after anaphylaxis. Which of the septic vasoplegia mechanisms would you expect to overlap with these states, and what differs?
questions.answer: Both are forms of vasodilatory shock, so the final pathway is similar: smooth muscle that is relaxed and responds poorly to catecholamines, with nitric oxide and potassium channel opening as plausible shared mechanisms. After bypass there is a systemic inflammatory response to the circuit, so the overlap with sepsis may be substantial, but there is no ongoing infection to remove. In anaphylaxis the main driver is mast cell mediators such as histamine, which act quickly and also cause marked capillary leak, so the onset is abrupt and the treatment of the cause is different. The reasoning about tone carries over; the reasoning about the cause does not.
questions.causalChain: Vasodilatory shock shares a final pathway of relaxed, poorly responsive smooth muscle; the trigger differs (infection, extracorporeal circuit, mast cell mediators); the trigger determines duration, leak and cause-directed treatment.
questions.assumption: That cardiac function is preserved in both cases.
questions.misconception: That all warm, hypotensive shock is septic.

principles.title: Part III. The veins: capacitance and stressed volume
body: The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-stressed-volume) showed that only part of the blood in the veins stretches their walls and creates mean systemic filling pressure, the pressure that drives venous return. That part is the stressed volume; the rest, which merely fills the veins without stretching them, is the unstressed volume. Venous tone decides how blood is divided between the two.

Sepsis lowers venous tone as well as arterial tone. When the veins relax, the same total blood volume holds a larger unstressed share and a smaller stressed share. Mean systemic filling pressure falls, venous return falls, and the circulation behaves as though it were empty even though no blood has been lost. This is sometimes called relative hypovolemia. Magder estimates that the stressed share is usually about 30 percent of total blood volume, a figure based on physiological estimates.

principles.title: Why fluid fills a bigger container
body: When the veins have relaxed, a fluid bolus first has to fill a container that has become larger. Some of the bolus raises stressed volume and mean systemic filling pressure, and venous return and stroke volume can rise. But two things then work against the gain. Part of the added volume settles into the relaxed, unstressed reservoir, and part leaves the circulation through a leaking capillary wall, which is the subject of Part IV.

So in sepsis a positive response to fluid is often partly transient. Stroke volume rises after the bolus and then drifts back as the extra volume redistributes. The fluid was not wrong, and the measured response was real, but the response alone does not show that the patient's problem was a lack of volume. In a patient whose main problem is lost venous tone, restoring tone addresses the cause, while fluid only fills the space the lost tone created.

questions.prompt: Patient V receives a fluid bolus. Her stroke volume rises, then falls back toward its starting value over the next hour. Predict why, using capacitance and leak.
questions.answer: The bolus raised her stressed volume and mean systemic filling pressure, so venous return and stroke volume rose. Over the next hour two things undid part of that. Her veins have lost tone, so some of the added volume settled into the enlarged unstressed reservoir without raising filling pressure. And her capillaries are leaking, so some of the fluid left the circulation into the tissues. Both lower stressed volume back toward where it was, and stroke volume follows.
questions.causalChain: Bolus raises stressed volume; mean systemic filling pressure and venous return rise; relaxed veins absorb volume into unstressed reservoir; capillary leak moves fluid out of the vessels; stressed volume falls back; stroke volume falls back.
questions.assumption: That her heart function and heart rate are stable over the hour.
questions.misconception: That a positive fluid response means more fluid will keep helping.

diagram.caption: Figure 2. Reused from the Shock chapter. In septic shock a positive stroke volume response to fluid can fade over the following hour, as volume moves into relaxed veins and out through leaking capillaries. A response shows that the heart can use the extra preload at that moment; it does not show how long the gain will last.
diagram.alt: The Shock chapter's fluid response figure, showing a curve of stroke volume against preload, with a steep part where added volume raises stroke volume and a flat part where it does not. In this chapter the caption adds that in sepsis the gain on the steep part can be temporary.

principles.title: How a vasopressor recruits unstressed volume
body: A vasopressor that constricts veins as well as arterioles moves blood from the unstressed to the stressed reservoir. In patients with septic shock, Persichini and colleagues found that norepinephrine raised mean systemic filling pressure, the effect summarized in the Shock chapter. The sepsis-specific consequence is that a vasopressor can do part of what fluid does, by restoring the venous tone that sepsis removed, without adding volume that could leak.

This also means that what looks like fluid responsiveness can sometimes be produced, or abolished, by a change in venous tone. A patient who responds to a bolus before a vasopressor is started may stop responding afterwards, because the vasopressor has already raised stressed volume. The response describes where the heart is on its curve at that moment, not a fixed property of the patient.

questions.prompt: A patient becomes hypotensive after spinal anesthesia, which blocks sympathetic outflow to the veins and arterioles of the lower body. Which part of septic physiology applies, and why might fluid behave differently?
questions.answer: The capacitance mechanism applies: loss of venous tone moves blood into the unstressed reservoir, lowers mean systemic filling pressure and reduces venous return, as in Patient V. But the capillary wall is intact, so fluid given stays in the vessels rather than leaking out, and the vasodilation wears off as the block recedes. Fluid would be expected to have a more lasting effect than in sepsis, and restoring tone with a vasoconstrictor addresses the cause directly.
questions.causalChain: Sympathetic block lowers venous tone; stressed volume and filling pressure fall; venous return falls; no inflammatory leak, so infused volume stays intravascular; the cause is temporary.
questions.assumption: That the patient is otherwise well, with a normal heart and no blood loss.
questions.misconception: That all hypotension caused by vasodilation behaves the same way when fluid is given.

principles.title: Part IV. The leaking capillary and where fluid goes
body: Fluid given into a vein is only useful to the circulation while it stays in the vessels. In health, the capillary wall holds most of it there for a time. In sepsis the wall becomes leakier, and a larger share of each bolus moves into the tissues, where it adds weight and edema rather than stressed volume. That is why, in sepsis, more fluid given is not the same as more circulating volume.

principles.title: The revised Starling principle and the glycocalyx
body: The classic Starling description had fluid filtered out at the arterial end of a capillary and reabsorbed at the venous end, driven by the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures. The revised Starling principle, set out by Woodcock and Woodcock among others, moves the key barrier to the endothelial glycocalyx, a gel-like layer of proteins and sugar chains lining the inner surface of the vessel. The oncotic pressure that matters is the one just beneath that layer, not the one in the surrounding tissue. One consequence of the revised model is what Woodcock and Woodcock call the no-absorption rule: in continuous capillaries, the type found in most tissues, the oncotic pressure difference opposes filtration but does not reverse it, so filtered fluid returns to the circulation mainly through the lymphatics. Some specialized capillaries, such as those of the kidney and gut, can absorb fluid.

In sepsis the glycocalyx is shed by enzymes activated by reactive oxygen species and inflammatory cytokines, and fragments of it can be measured in the blood, where they may serve as biomarkers. That shedding is observed. How much of septic capillary leak it explains in humans, and whether any treatment protects or restores it, are uncertain. This chapter treats the glycocalyx as a well-supported explanation for why the barrier fails, not as a target for any therapy.

principles.title: Patient L: where 6 liters went
body: Patient L shows the cost of fluid that does not stay. Over 24 hours he received a net positive balance of 6 L, his weight rose by 6 kg, and his hemoglobin fell from 13 to 10.5 g/dL without bleeding. The fall in hemoglobin is dilution: his red cells are spread through a larger plasma volume. Working backwards from that dilution gives a rough sense of how much of the fluid is still in his vessels.

The estimate in the worked example suggests that about 1.3 L, roughly 22 percent of the 6 L, is still circulating. That figure is an illustrative teaching estimate built on stated assumptions. It is not a measured value, and it is not the amount that leaks in sepsis generally. For comparison only, Hahn reports from volume kinetic studies, mostly in people without sepsis, that crystalloid expands plasma by about 15 to 20 percent of the infused volume within 30 minutes after an infusion ends. The two figures are similar in size, but Hahn's is not the source of Patient L's estimate. The rest of the fluid is mostly in the interstitium, where it carries organ costs: in the lungs it widens the distance oxygen must cross and raises his oxygen requirement, in the gut wall it raises interstitial pressure, and in a kidney enclosed by its capsule it can raise tissue pressure. Patient L's rising oxygen need is the clearest of these costs at the bedside.

diagram.caption: Figure 3. Where fluid goes when the capillary leaks. Schematic of fluid given into the circulation, with part staying in the vessels and most moving into the interstitium of lung, gut and kidney, and an inset of an intact and a shed glycocalyx. Schematic only; no proportions are shown.
diagram.alt: A schematic of a blood vessel with fluid entering from an intravenous line. Arrows show some fluid remaining in the vessel and more fluid passing through the vessel wall into the surrounding tissue, labeled lung, gut and kidney. An inset shows two magnified sections of vessel lining, one with a thick intact glycocalyx layer and one with a thin, patchy layer. No numbers or proportions are shown.

workedExample.title: Worked example: Patient L's dilution estimate (illustrative teaching estimate)
body: Starting blood volume: 70 mL/kg x 80 kg = 5.6 L.
If red cell mass is unchanged, hemoglobin falls in proportion to the rise in blood volume. New blood volume = 5.6 x 13 / 10.5, about 6.93 L. The rise is about 1.3 L.
Fraction of the 6 L net balance still intravascular: 1.3 / 6, about 22 percent.

Assumptions: no bleeding, no blood sampling loss, unchanged red cell mass, a single well-mixed compartment, and an assumed starting blood volume. Each assumption is uncertain, so this is an illustrative teaching estimate, not a measurement of leak, and it is not used in any figure.

principles.title: What the fluid trials show
body: Two trials already cited in the Shock chapter tested how much fluid to give. CLASSIC compared restrictive with standard intravenous fluid in adults in intensive care with septic shock who had already received initial resuscitation. CLOVERS compared a restrictive strategy, relying earlier on vasopressors, with a more liberal fluid strategy in adults with sepsis-induced hypotension after initial fluid, most of them enrolled in the emergency department. Neither trial found a significant difference in its primary outcome: death at 90 days in CLASSIC, and death before discharge home by day 90 in CLOVERS.

What the trials show is that, within the range of strategies they tested, giving less fluid did not lead to more deaths, and giving more did not lead to fewer. They do not show that fluid is harmful, that any single bolus is harmful, or that fluid should be withheld from a patient who is clearly underfilled. They tested strategies across populations, not the response of one patient to one bolus. The [Shock chapter's](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-fluid-responsiveness) distinction between fluid responsiveness and fluid tolerance is what lets a clinician apply them to the patient in front of them.

questions.prompt: Patient L has no rise in stroke volume with a passive leg raise. Predict the effect of another fluid bolus on his cardiac output and on his oxygenation.
questions.answer: His cardiac output would probably not rise. A leg raise that does not increase stroke volume suggests his heart is on the flat part of its curve, where extra preload is not converted into more output. Much of the bolus would also leak, because his capillaries are leaking. His oxygenation would be expected to worsen, because more fluid would move into his lungs, which are already wet. Another bolus has little expected benefit and a likely cost.
questions.causalChain: No leg-raise response suggests a flat Starling curve; added preload does not raise stroke volume; leaking capillaries move much of the bolus into tissue; lung water rises; gas exchange worsens.
questions.assumption: That the leg raise was done correctly and stroke volume was measured accurately, and that his abdominal pressure is not high enough to make the test unreliable.
questions.misconception: That a patient on a vasopressor always needs more fluid.

questions.prompt: A colleague says CLASSIC proves that fluids are harmful in septic shock. What does the trial show, and what does it not show?
questions.answer: CLASSIC compared restrictive with standard fluid in adults in intensive care with septic shock after initial resuscitation, and found no significant difference in mortality. That supports the safety of a restrictive approach in that population, at that stage. It does not show that fluid is harmful, because the more liberal arm did not do worse in a statistically significant way. It also does not apply directly to the first hours of resuscitation, to a patient who is clearly underfilled, or to the effect of a single bolus given as a test.
questions.causalChain: Trial compared two strategies after initial resuscitation; no significant mortality difference; a null result does not show harm from either arm; population and timing limit how far it applies.
questions.assumption: That the patients in front of you resemble the trial population: adults in intensive care with septic shock who had already received initial fluid.
questions.misconception: That a trial without a significant difference proves one arm is harmful.

questions.prompt: A patient has severe burns, and another severe acute pancreatitis. What from Patient L carries over, and what differs?
questions.answer: Both conditions cause a systemic inflammatory response with increased capillary permeability, so the central point carries over: fluid given into the vessels leaves them, edema carries organ costs, and the fraction that stays is smaller than in health. In burns, large volumes are also lost directly from the damaged skin, and fluid needs in the early hours are driven by that loss as well as by leak. In pancreatitis, fluid collects in the abdomen and can raise abdominal pressure, which compresses veins and organs. The leak reasoning applies; the sources of loss and where the fluid collects differ.
questions.causalChain: Inflammation raises permeability; infused fluid moves into tissue; edema raises interstitial pressure in organs; burns add direct surface loss; pancreatitis adds abdominal collection and pressure.
questions.assumption: That neither patient has ongoing bleeding.
questions.misconception: That large fluid needs always mean that more fluid is still helping.

principles.title: Part V. Heterogeneous flow and cellular dysfunction
body: Parts II to IV dealt with mechanisms that are well established: lost arterial tone, lost venous tone and capillary leak. This Part moves to the microcirculation and the cells, where the evidence is weaker and the explanations are less settled. Each section is labeled with how firmly its claims are supported. Established means the finding is consistently shown in patients and broadly accepted. Observed means it has been seen directly in patients, but its causal role is not proven. Hypothesis means it is a proposed explanation supported by experimental or indirect data. Nothing in this Part is presented as a treatment target.

principles.title: Heterogeneous microvascular flow (observed)
body: Status: observed. Using orthogonal polarization spectral imaging of the small vessels under the tongue, De Backer and colleagues found that microvascular flow in 50 patients with what was then called severe sepsis, a pre-Sepsis-3 category, was altered, with fewer perfused small vessels and more vessels with stopped or intermittent flow than in controls. Flow was heterogeneous: some capillaries were well perfused while their neighbors were not. In that study, the alterations were more severe in patients who died. That is an association with outcome, not proof that the alterations caused death.

Ince has described, in what he calls a personal viewpoint, the idea of hemodynamic coherence: in health, restoring pressure and cardiac output restores flow in the small vessels, but in sepsis that link can break, so that the large-vessel numbers are corrected while the microcirculation stays disordered. Status: a framework for interpreting monitoring, not an established finding. Whether loss of coherence causes organ failure, and whether any treatment aimed at the microcirculation improves outcome, are uncertain.

diagram.caption: Figure 4. Loss of hemodynamic coherence (observed association, not a causal model). Large-vessel variables such as MAP and cardiac output are restored, while flow in the small vessels stays heterogeneous, with some capillaries perfused and others not. Conceptual only.
diagram.alt: Two panels. The left panel shows a gauge for MAP and cardiac output moving into the normal range. The right panel shows a network of capillaries in which some are filled with moving red cells and others are empty or show stopped flow. A label reads observed association, not a causal model.

principles.title: Impaired cellular oxygen use (hypothesis)
body: Status: hypothesis. Singer and others have proposed that in sepsis the mitochondria in some cells use oxygen less effectively, so that organs fail even when enough oxygen reaches them. Supporting data come from experimental models and from observational studies in patients. The idea would explain why organ dysfunction can persist after the circulation is restored, and why organs that fail in sepsis often recover with little lasting damage, which has been interpreted as a protective shutdown rather than cell death.

This remains a hypothesis. It is not established in human septic shock as a cause of organ failure, and it is not a treatment target. It is included because it offers one possible explanation for findings that the circulation alone does not fully explain, and because the plan for this chapter requires that uncertain cellular explanations be kept separate from established ones.

principles.title: Lactate in sepsis (established that it is not only hypoxic)
body: The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-extraction-lactate) showed that lactate rises when oxygen delivery falls below what the tissues need, but that it can also rise for other reasons. Sepsis is the clearest case. Patient V has a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L while her global oxygen delivery is high.

Her arterial oxygen content is 1.34 x 12 x 0.94 + 0.003 x 70, about 15.3 mL/dL, and her delivery is 75 dL/min x 15.3, about 1150 mL/min, well above normal. A high lactate with that delivery cannot be explained by a global shortage of oxygen. Reviews by Garcia-Alvarez and colleagues and by Suetrong and Walley describe other contributors in sepsis: adrenergic stimulation of glycolysis in well-oxygenated cells, particularly muscle, and reduced lactate clearance by the liver. Regional underperfusion may also contribute, as the heterogeneous flow described above suggests. Status: that sepsis-associated hyperlactatemia is not explained by hypoxia alone is established; how much each contributor matters in a given patient is uncertain.

principles.title: Capillary refill as a perfusion signal (trial evidence)
body: Status: trial evidence. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK compared a resuscitation strategy aimed at normalizing capillary refill time with one aimed at normalizing lactate in early septic shock. Its primary outcome, 28-day mortality, did not differ significantly between the groups. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2, already cited in the Shock chapter, tested personalized resuscitation guided by capillary refill time against usual care. It found the capillary refill-guided strategy superior to usual care on a combined 28-day outcome of death, duration of vital organ support and length of hospital stay (win ratio 1.16, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.33, P = .04), driven mainly by shorter organ support. Mortality at 28 days was the same in both groups, 26.5% vs 26.6%. Neither trial shows that capillary refill-guided resuscitation saves lives.

The physiological point is narrower than the trials. Capillary refill is a bedside signal of skin perfusion that changes within minutes, while lactate is a whole-body signal that changes over hours and has several sources, as Patient V shows. The two can disagree, and when they do, each is answering a different question.

questions.prompt: Patient V's MAP and cardiac output have been restored and her capillary refill has normalized, but over 2 hours her lactate rises from 4.2 to 4.8 mmol/L. Predict the possible explanations, in order of likelihood, and say what would separate them.
questions.answer: First, ongoing adrenergic stimulation of glycolysis, from her illness and any catecholamine she is receiving, in tissue that is not short of oxygen. Second, reduced clearance by the liver. Third, regional underperfusion that the skin does not reveal, for example in the gut, or heterogeneous microvascular flow. Less likely, an undrained source of infection or a new complication. A falling vasopressor requirement and improving organ function would favor the first two; a worsening abdomen, rising vasopressor need, or a new source on imaging would favor regional hypoperfusion or an uncontrolled source. A single lactate value cannot separate them; its trend alongside the other signals can.
questions.causalChain: Lactate has several sources in sepsis; restored global flow and normal skin perfusion make global oxygen shortage unlikely; adrenergic glycolysis and reduced clearance can raise lactate in well-oxygenated tissue; regional hypoperfusion remains possible.
questions.assumption: That the lactate measurements are accurate and from the same type of sample.
questions.misconception: That a rising lactate always means that oxygen delivery is too low.

questions.prompt: A patient after cardiac arrest has a normal MAP but slow capillary refill. Which of this Part's septic concepts apply, and which do not?
questions.answer: Loss of coherence may apply: after cardiac arrest the large-vessel numbers can be restored while small-vessel flow remains disordered, and the post-arrest state includes a systemic inflammatory response. Lactate interpretation also carries over, because a rising lactate after arrest can have several sources. What does not carry over directly is the septic cause: there is no infection to treat, and the post-arrest heart is often stunned, so slow refill may reflect low cardiac output or vasoconstriction rather than heterogeneous flow. Status labels apply here too; none of these is established as a treatment target after arrest.
questions.causalChain: Normal pressure does not guarantee skin perfusion; coherence can be lost after any severe inflammatory insult; slow refill can reflect low flow, high tone or microcirculatory disorder; causes differ between arrest and sepsis.
questions.assumption: That the patient is normothermic, since cold skin slows capillary refill on its own.
questions.misconception: That a normal MAP means the tissues are well perfused.

principles.title: Part VI. The septic heart
body: Patient B in the Shock chapter showed that warm skin can hide a weak heart. Patient C shows the same thing further along. His peripheries are cold and his capillary refill is slow, but the decisive finding is on echocardiography: a globally hypokinetic left ventricle in a man whose septic shock might otherwise have been treated as a problem of tone and volume alone.

principles.title: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy
body: Status: established that it occurs and is usually reversible. Sepsis can depress contraction of both ventricles, and in survivors the depression usually recovers over days to weeks. Hollenberg and Singer review its features and proposed mechanisms. It is common, but this chapter gives no percentage, because published estimates vary with the definition, the imaging and the population studied.

Status: partly established, partly hypothesis. The proposed mechanisms include circulating inflammatory mediators that depress contraction, nitric oxide acting on the heart muscle, disordered calcium handling inside the cells, and mitochondrial dysfunction of the kind described in Part V. Some of these have direct support in patients and some rest mainly on experimental work. The working picture is of a heart that is not dead but temporarily switched down, which is consistent with its usual recovery.

principles.title: Patient C in numbers
body: Patient C's numbers contrast with Patient V's at every step. His stroke volume is 26 mL against her 64, his SVR about 1250 against her 500, and his oxygen delivery about 455 mL/min against her 1150. His tissues are compensating by extracting a larger share of the oxygen they receive, which is why his ScvO2 is low.

These numbers place Patient C's main problem in the pump, not in the vessels. His high SVR is the expected response to a low output: his arterioles are constricting to hold pressure, which is the opposite of Patient V's vasoplegia. Adding more constriction would ask a weak ventricle to pump against even more resistance.

workedExample.title: Worked example: Patient C's oxygen delivery and extraction
body: Arterial content: CaO2 = 1.34 x 11 x 0.95 + 0.003 x 80 = 14.0 + 0.24, about 14.2 mL/dL.
Delivery: DO2 = 32 dL/min x 14.2, about 455 mL/min.
Venous content, using ScvO2 as a stand-in for mixed venous saturation and ignoring dissolved oxygen: CvO2 = 1.34 x 11 x 0.55, about 8.1 mL/dL.
Consumption: VO2 = 32 x (14.2 - 8.1), about 195 mL/min. Extraction = 195 / 455, about 43 percent.
For comparison, Patient V: CaO2 about 15.3 mL/dL and DO2 about 1150 mL/min. These are illustrative numbers, and central venous saturation is only an approximation of mixed venous saturation.

principles.title: The cost of raising pressure in a weak heart
body: A healthy ventricle can maintain its stroke volume when afterload rises. A weak one often cannot: as the pressure it must pump against rises, its stroke volume falls. The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-pressors-inotropes) describes this interaction; in Patient C it means that raising MAP with a vasoconstrictor alone may raise pressure while lowering flow, so that the number on the monitor improves while delivery to the tissues falls.

This is where the reasoning points toward support for contraction, with inotropic agents, rather than more constriction. The evidence is thin. No randomized trial has shown that an inotrope improves outcomes in septic cardiomyopathy. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline addresses inotropes and advises against levosimendan, and LeoPARDS, a trial of levosimendan in septic shock, did not show less organ dysfunction or lower mortality and found more supraventricular tachyarrhythmias. This chapter gives no doses and no order of use. The physiological point stands on its own: in a patient like Patient C, pressure and flow must be assessed separately, because treatment aimed at one can worsen the other.

questions.prompt: Patient C's MAP is raised from 64 to 75 mm Hg with a vasoconstrictor alone. Predict the direction of change in his stroke volume, cardiac output, ScvO2 and capillary refill.
questions.answer: His stroke volume is likely to fall or at best stay level, because a weak ventricle cannot maintain its output against a higher afterload. His cardiac output would fall with it, or stay level if his heart rate rises. With less flow and the same oxygen consumption, his tissues would extract more, so his ScvO2 would be expected to fall further. His capillary refill would be expected to stay slow or lengthen, because skin vessels constrict further and flow falls. The pressure gain could hide a fall in delivery.
questions.causalChain: Vasoconstrictor raises afterload; a depressed ventricle loses stroke volume as afterload rises; output falls; extraction rises and ScvO2 falls; skin vasoconstriction and lower flow slow capillary refill.
questions.assumption: That his heart rate and filling stay roughly the same and that the agent has no direct effect on contraction.
questions.misconception: That a higher MAP always means a better circulation.

questions.prompt: A patient presents with fever and a weak left ventricle, and the eventual diagnosis is takotsubo syndrome or myocarditis rather than sepsis. Where does the septic-heart reasoning help, and where does it mislead?
questions.answer: It helps with the hemodynamics: a weak ventricle with a low stroke volume and high SVR responds poorly to more afterload, and pressure and flow need separate assessment, whatever the cause. It misleads if it anchors the clinician on infection. Fever and a weak heart do not prove sepsis, and searching for a source and giving antimicrobials do not treat myocarditis or takotsubo. The recovery pattern may also differ. Whether the cause is septic has to be decided by the history, the tests and the course, not by the hemodynamic pattern.
questions.causalChain: Depressed ventricle plus high afterload gives low output regardless of cause; fever can accompany non-infective myocardial disease; the cause determines specific treatment; hemodynamic pattern alone cannot identify the cause.
questions.assumption: That the patient's ventricular function has been assessed by imaging.
questions.misconception: That a febrile patient with shock always has septic shock.

principles.title: Part VII. Treating the cause: source and time
body: Everything in Parts II to VI buys time. Vasopressors restore tone, fluid restores volume for a while, and support for the heart restores flow. None of them removes the infection that is driving the host response. Only antimicrobials and, where there is a removable source, source control do that.

principles.title: Antimicrobial timing: association, not proof
body: Kumar and colleagues, in a retrospective study of patients with septic shock, found that each hour of delay in effective antimicrobial therapy after the onset of hypotension was associated with lower survival. Seymour and colleagues, using data from the mandated sepsis program in New York State, found that longer time to completion of the sepsis bundle and to antibiotics was associated with higher mortality. Both are observational. Patients who are treated later differ from those treated early in ways that are hard to measure, such as how obvious their sepsis was at presentation, so the size of any effect is uncertain.

The physiological reasoning is straightforward: as long as the organisms keep multiplying, they keep driving the host response that Parts II to VI describe. The current Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline, published in 2026, makes recommendations about antimicrobial timing. This chapter does not quote them or their strength.

principles.title: Why a drained collection changes the physiology
body: An abscess, an infected gallbladder or an obstructed and infected urinary tract contains organisms and inflammatory products in a space that antimicrobials penetrate poorly. As long as it remains, it keeps feeding the host response. Draining or removing it takes away that input. The circulation can then recover as tone returns, leak slows and the heart recovers, which no amount of support achieves while the source keeps driving the response.

Patient C has a gallbladder source that has not yet been drained. His circulation, however well supported, is being pushed in the wrong direction by an input that is still there. This chapter does not discuss how or when source control should be done, and it quotes no timing recommendation; that is a matter for the guideline and for surgical judgement.

questions.prompt: Patient C receives appropriate antimicrobials, but his gallbladder is not drained for 24 hours. Predict his vasopressor need and lactate over that day, and why.
questions.answer: His vasopressor need is likely to stay high or rise, and his lactate is likely to stay high or rise, despite appropriate antimicrobials. The undrained gallbladder keeps supplying organisms and inflammatory products to the host response, so arterial and venous tone stay low, leak continues and his heart remains depressed. Antimicrobials may slow the process but penetrate the collection poorly. Improvement would be expected mainly after drainage.
questions.causalChain: Undrained source keeps driving the host response; vasoplegia, leak and myocardial depression persist; antimicrobials penetrate the collection poorly; support holds the numbers but does not reverse the cause.
questions.assumption: That the chosen antimicrobials are active against the organisms and that no other source is present.
questions.misconception: That starting antimicrobials is enough to control any source.

questions.prompt: A patient has a necrotizing soft tissue infection. Why does the reasoning of this Part make source control more urgent rather than less?
questions.answer: Dead and dying tissue has no blood supply, so antimicrobials barely reach it, and the infection can spread along tissue planes faster than the circulation can be supported. The source keeps growing while it remains, so the host response is driven harder every hour. Supportive treatment can hold the numbers briefly but cannot reach the cause. Removing the tissue is the only way to remove the input.
questions.causalChain: Necrotic tissue is unperfused; antimicrobials do not reach it; infection spreads; the inflammatory input grows; only removal stops it.
questions.assumption: That the diagnosis is correct and that the patient can tolerate surgery.
questions.misconception: That a patient must be hemodynamically stable before the source is dealt with.

principles.title: Part VIII. Support, its limits, and reassessment
body: Support keeps the patient alive while the cause is treated. It works on some levels of the circulation and not others, so each form of support helps up to a point and then stops. Reading the response means asking three separate questions, about pressure, about flow and about the organs, because a treatment can improve one while worsening another.

principles.title: What tone loss means for a pressure target
body: The [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-pressors-inotropes) covers the mean arterial pressure target and the trials behind it, SEPSISPAM and the trial by Lamontagne and colleagues in older adults. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline strongly recommends an initial MAP target of 65 mm Hg over higher targets (Recommendation 13), and for patients aged 65 and over it conditionally suggests a target of 60 to 65 mm Hg (Recommendation 14).

What lost tone adds is a reason why a pressure target is a floor, not a goal. Below a certain pressure, organs whose autoregulation is impaired by sepsis lose flow as pressure falls. Above that floor, more pressure bought with more constriction does not guarantee more flow, as Patient V's falling output and Patient C's afterload problem show. The target sets the minimum the circulation must provide; the other signals show whether it is enough.

principles.title: Adjunct treatments and what the trials tested
body: Several treatments have been tested because they act on a mechanism that catecholamines do not. Vasopressin replaces a hormone that may be relatively deficient and acts through non-adrenergic receptors. VASST compared vasopressin with norepinephrine in adults with septic shock already receiving norepinephrine and found no significant difference in mortality, its primary outcome. A possible difference in a less severely ill subgroup was not supported by a significant test for heterogeneity and is hypothesis-generating only. Corticosteroids are thought to restore vascular responsiveness to catecholamines and to modulate the host response. ADRENAL tested hydrocortisone in adults with septic shock who were receiving mechanical ventilation, and enrolled only such patients. It found no significant difference in mortality at 90 days, its primary outcome, although shock resolved faster with hydrocortisone. APROCCHSS tested hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in adults with septic shock in intensive care and found significantly lower mortality at 90 days, its primary outcome; the difference at 28 days was not significant. Angiotensin II acts through its own receptor and replaces a constricting signal. ATHOS-3 tested it in adults with vasodilatory shock that persisted despite high vasopressor requirements, most but not all of whom had sepsis, and found that more patients reached its blood pressure goal with angiotensin II. That primary outcome was a pressure response, and the trial did not show a significant difference in mortality.

Among these trials, only APROCCHSS showed a significant mortality difference. The results are stated qualitatively here, and no doses or order of use are given. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline makes conditional suggestions about adding vasopressin and epinephrine in septic shock; it makes no recommendation for angiotensin II. The physiological lesson is that a drug can act on a real mechanism and raise pressure without improving survival, and that two trials of a similar treatment can reach different conclusions when their populations and interventions differ.

questions.prompt: ADRENAL and APROCCHSS reached different conclusions about mortality with corticosteroids in septic shock. What differed between the trials, and what can a reader conclude?
questions.answer: The interventions differed: ADRENAL tested hydrocortisone alone, while APROCCHSS added fludrocortisone, a mineralocorticoid. The populations also differed: ADRENAL enrolled only patients receiving mechanical ventilation, while APROCCHSS enrolled adults in intensive care within 24 hours of septic shock. APROCCHSS's mortality difference was significant at 90 days but not at 28 days. A reader can conclude that corticosteroids act on a real mechanism and appear to speed resolution of shock, but that a mortality benefit depends on details of the population and the regimen that two trials cannot settle on their own. The trials do not support a simple statement that steroids work or do not work.
questions.causalChain: Two trials of a related intervention; different regimens and populations; one shows a mortality benefit and one does not; a difference in design limits direct comparison; mechanism and pressure effects do not guarantee survival benefit.
questions.assumption: That each trial's primary outcome, mortality at 90 days, is the right measure for comparing them.
questions.misconception: That a trial without a mortality benefit means the treatment has no physiological effect.

principles.title: Three separate questions
body: For each patient, three questions need separate answers. Is the pressure enough? Is the flow enough? Are the organs recovering? Pressure is read from MAP. Flow is read from cardiac output where it is measured, and indirectly from capillary refill, ScvO2 and the lactate trend. Organ recovery is read from mental state, urine output, gas exchange and the trend in organ function tests.

In Patient V, pressure is the first problem and flow is already high, so the question is whether her organs recover as tone is restored and her source is treated. In Patient L, pressure is held, but his organs are paying for the fluid that leaked, so the question is whether flow can be maintained without adding more. In Patient C, pressure is near target while flow is low, so the question is whether flow can be raised and his source removed. The [Shock chapter's final return](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-final-return) used the same three questions.

questions.prompt: After source control, Patient V's vasopressor need falls over 12 hours. Predict which signals improve first and why.
questions.answer: Her vasopressor need and pressure improve first, because arteriolar and venous tone recover as the inflammatory drive falls. Capillary refill, already normal, should stay so. Her lactate would be expected to fall more slowly, because clearance takes time and adrenergic stimulation falls only as her vasopressor need falls. Organ function, such as renal function, would be expected to recover last, over days, because organs recover more slowly than vessels respond.
questions.causalChain: Source control removes the inflammatory input; vascular tone recovers within hours; vasopressor need falls; lactate falls more slowly with clearance and reduced adrenergic drive; organ function recovers over days.
questions.assumption: That no new complication occurs and that her heart remains normal.
questions.misconception: That a falling lactate is the first sign of recovery.

questions.prompt: A patient with septic shock also has chronic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction. Which of the three questions becomes hardest to answer, and why?
questions.answer: Flow becomes hardest. The patient's baseline output is already low, so a low output now may reflect the chronic condition, new septic depression or underfilling, and the usual signals overlap: a slow capillary refill, a low ScvO2 and a raised lactate can all come from the chronic state. The heart also tolerates both fluid and afterload poorly, so each test of flow carries more risk. Pressure is still read directly, and organ recovery can be judged against the patient's baseline, but flow needs a direct measurement more than in most patients.
questions.causalChain: Chronic low output confounds the signals of flow; septic depression adds to it; fluid and afterload are poorly tolerated; indirect markers overlap with the chronic state; direct flow measurement becomes more important.
questions.assumption: That the patient's baseline ejection fraction and function are known.
questions.misconception: That a patient with heart failure should never receive fluid in sepsis.

principles.title: Back to the three patients
body: Patient V's circulation failed at the arterioles and veins. Her heart was strong and her flow high, and her pressure was low because the vessels had lost their tone. Restoring tone addressed her mechanism; fluid helped only briefly, because her veins and capillaries let it go. Patient L's circulation failed at the capillary wall. His pressure was held, but the fluid that kept it there had moved into his lungs and other organs, and his heart was no longer able to use more. Patient C's circulation failed at the heart. His vessels were constricted to hold a pressure his weak ventricle could barely produce, and adding more constriction risked lowering flow further. All three needed treatment of the cause, and Patient C needed his source removed.
One label covered all three. The level that sepsis attacked most determined which support helped and which harmed.

principles.title: Synthesis
body: Sepsis attacks the circulation at four levels: arteriolar tone, venous capacitance, the capillary wall, and the heart and cells. The first three are well established; the microcirculatory and cellular explanations are observed or hypothetical and are not treatment targets. Fluids, vasopressors and support for the heart each act on some of these levels and not others, so each helps up to a point and then stops. Only antimicrobials and source control remove the cause. The trials tested strategies in populations; the physiology is what lets a clinician decide which level is failing in the patient in front of them.

treatmentApproach.title: Recognize septic shock by organs and perfusion
treatmentApproach.action: Look for organ dysfunction and signs of poor perfusion, not only a low blood pressure. Note whether the peripheries are warm or cold and how long capillary refill takes.
treatmentApproach.why: The label identifies risk, not the hemodynamic type; patients with the same pressure and shock index can have opposite circulations.

treatmentApproach.title: Start treating the infection and look for a removable source
treatmentApproach.action: Start treatment of the infection and look early for a collection, obstruction or dead tissue that can be drained or removed.
treatmentApproach.why: Support buys time; only antimicrobials and source control remove the driver of the host response.

treatmentApproach.title: Restore perfusion pressure, then ask which level is failing
treatmentApproach.action: Restore a minimum perfusion pressure. Before adding more of anything, decide whether the main problem is lost tone, lost volume or a weak heart.
treatmentApproach.why: Fluid, vasopressors and support for contraction each act on different levels; the wrong one can raise a number while worsening flow.

treatmentApproach.title: Treat each fluid bolus as a test
treatmentApproach.action: State the response you expect from each bolus and the cost you will watch for, such as rising oxygen need. Stop when the response stops.
treatmentApproach.why: In sepsis much of each bolus leaks, responses are often transient, and edema raises tissue pressure in the lungs and other organs.

treatmentApproach.title: Assess flow when the response does not fit
treatmentApproach.action: When pressure improves but perfusion does not, or the heart may be weak, assess cardiac function and flow directly rather than relying on pressure.
treatmentApproach.why: A vasoconstrictor can raise pressure and lower output in a weak heart; pressure alone cannot show it.

treatmentApproach.title: Reassess pressure, flow and organs separately
treatmentApproach.action: Recheck pressure, flow signals and organ function as three questions, and act on each against the level you think is failing.
treatmentApproach.why: A treatment can improve one of the three while worsening another; signals change on different timescales.
